title: The Overloaded Database
summary: 5,000 reads per second are crushing a database that tops out at 1,000. Take the pressure off without rewriting the app.
scenario: Your product page went viral. Traffic jumped to 5,000 requests per second, and almost all of them are reads of the same popular items.
The app servers are fine: you already scaled them out. The single SQL database can only handle about 1,000 queries per second, so about four in five requests are failing.
Get the database back under control. Most of the traffic hits a small set of hot keys, which is a strong clue.

functional: Read product details from the SQL database
Keep the existing app servers and data model (no rewrite)
nonFunctional: Handle 5,000 reads/s at peak, 90% on a few hot items
Database load at or below 800 rps (20% headroom)
Average latency at or below 60 ms

objectives.label: Database load at or below 800 rps (leave 20% headroom)
Average latency at or below 60 ms

hints: Run the simulation first and read the bottleneck list. Which component is red, and how far over capacity is it?
90% of reads hit hot keys. A component that answers repeated reads from memory would stop most of them from ever reaching the database.
Connect a Redis Cache to the Catalog API. With an 8 GB cache too many reads still miss, so increase the cache size until database load drops below 800 rps (around 24 GB or more).
explanation: Read-heavy workloads with a skewed key distribution are the classic case for cache-aside. The app checks the cache first and only goes to the database on a miss, then fills the cache.
Database load becomes reads × (1 − hit ratio). At 5,000 rps and an 87% hit ratio, the database sees about 650 rps, comfortably under its 1,000 rps limit.

Cache size matters: a small cache can't hold enough of the working set, so the hit ratio plateaus. In real systems you would also think about TTLs, invalidation on writes, and stampede protection when a hot key expires.

Read replicas are the other lever. They add read capacity but not write capacity, and they cost a full database each. Here a cache is far cheaper per request served. Adding Monitoring and a second cache replica would remove the remaining reliability risks.
